passage: When Pankaj was nine, his green parrot flew out of the window. "He'll be back tomorrow," he told his sister Farida, and put out a bowl of seeds by the gate. The next day the bowl was untouched. The next day too. His father Gautam sat beside him and said, "Maybe he will, maybe he won't. Either way I'll help you look." Pankaj cried hard, wrapped in a blanket, then agreed to draw a picture for lost-pet posters. At fifteen, Pankaj had a maths test coming and told everyone, "I'm sure to fail. I'll be lucky to pass." He told his friends the same about science and Hindi. When results arrived, a good mark in maths felt like a gift, and a low one in science hardly stung. But Farida noticed that he had left his textbooks shut, because what would be the point. "You say you'll fail so it won't hurt," she said. "You don't actually think that, do you?" Pankaj shrugged and stared at the ceiling.

qa.q: What did Pankaj put out by the gate for the parrot?
qa.a: He put out a bowl of seeds by the gate.

qa.q: How do Pankaj's expectations at nine and fifteen differ, and what do they share?
qa.a: At nine he was sure the parrot would come back tomorrow, and it hurt when it did not, while at fifteen he expected to fail every exam so any mark felt like a win. Both protect his feelings, but the second also quietly cut his effort.

qa.q: What was Pankaj feeling when he cried hard, wrapped in a blanket, after several days without the parrot?
qa.a: He felt heartbroken and shocked because his hope had been so certain.

qa.q: What could Farida say or do to help Pankaj with his exams?
qa.a: She could ask him what result he really hopes for and offer to study with him, so effort does not stop.

grounding: The same person shows two ways of guarding feelings: a child's fixed rosy view that shatters, and a teenager's defensive pessimism that lowers his effort.
